name: Nora Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Nora. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach the mixed class of five to seven-year-olds at Ashby Green Primary, a village school with sixty-two children and three classrooms. My day is reading books, number lines, the vegetable patch and dinner duty, because there are only four of us to do everything. I love that I know every family, and I see the children at Sunday school too. What wears me out is that the county keeps talking about closing us and sending the children on a bus to the town school.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does money work for you at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my boyfriend Mark in a little rented cottage on the edge of the village, and Mark works on his parents' sheep farm for not much more than his keep. I'm on lower pay because a small school can't give allowances, and we have less than a month of money saved. If Ashby Green shuts, the nearest school is the town one, and they're not hiring. I use AI now and then, mainly for the weekly newsletter to parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a relief, and that people should stop worrying and get on with it. I'd say it at the school gate and at the village hall coffee morning. I'd mention I find it handy for the newsletter, nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, AI isn't my worry, the county is. Small schools like ours are always on the list, and numbers are falling because young families can't afford to live in the village. Nothing changing with AI doesn't stop them closing us in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching and keep the newsletter tool, it saves me an hour on Fridays. I'd help the parents' group campaign to keep the school open, letters to the county, a petition at the shop. And Mark and I would try to put fifty pounds a month aside, in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but used to it. Like living near a river that floods every few winters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said young families can't afford the village. What would it take to keep the school open?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More children, honestly. Ten more and we're safe. The county counts heads, not how good the school is, so we're always one bad year away from closing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if it closed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to the town school, and to supply teaching, which is day-by-day cover work. Mark can't leave the farm, so moving isn't really an option. That's what scares me, we're tied here.

I'd say AI is handy for the **newsletter**, nothing more.
think: Her real worry is the **county closing** small schools, not AI.
Falling **pupil numbers** could shut Ashby Green within two years.
do: Keep using the **newsletter tool** to save an hour on Fridays.
Help the parents' **campaign** to keep the school open.
Save **fifty pounds a month** with her boyfriend.
feel: **Uneasy** but used to it, like living near a river that floods.
S0.quote: The county counts heads, not how good the school is, so we're always one bad year away from closing.
fieldNote: Nora's main threat is a **school closure**, which exists without AI.
She's **tied** to the village because her boyfriend works on the family farm.
She uses AI in a **small, practical** way for the newsletter.

steps.text: Keep using the AI newsletter tool on Fridays
Collect petition signatures at the village shop
Save fifty pounds a month with Mark

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say every school should be careful, but if it helps small schools stay open, good. I'd say the people who run schools need to show it works before forcing it on everyone. I'd be practical about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the county would use AI to justify closing us: remote lessons, one teacher across two villages, a screen for the rest. The thinking bits of my day, planning and reports, could go to AI, which sounds nice until it's the excuse to cut a teacher. With less than a month saved and only one other school nearby, that's serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools properly, once the town school is using them, so I can show I'm worth keeping. I'd ask Mark's parents if we could move into the old farmhouse annexe rent-free if things got tight. And I'd keep fighting the closure through the parish council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like the night before a big inspection when you know they've already decided.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd show you're worth keeping. How?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By being the teacher who can do the AI part and still know every child. Mrs Pryce, our head, is retiring in two years, and if I can show I'd run it well, maybe they'd keep me on. A village school without a teacher who knows the families is just a bus stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving into Mark's family's annexe, how would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, honestly. Family helping family is how it should work. His mum would want me to help with the lambing, which I don't mind.

steps.text: Learn the town school's AI tools in the first term

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and someone should have thought about families first. I'd say communities will have to look after each other. I wouldn't expect the government to save us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, by 2028 I think village schools close or go remote, with a teaching assistant and a screen. My job as I know it would be gone, and with less than a month saved, we'd struggle within weeks. Sheep don't care about AI, so my boyfriend's family farm would carry on for a while, until the robots come around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move onto the farm straight away to save rent. I'd apply for any job that's still about being with children, nursery work or teaching assistant, even on less pay. And I'd help with lambing and the farm shop, so at least the family income holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like seeing smoke from the village and not knowing whose house it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the children at Ashby Green in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd get a bus to town, or a screen at home. The little ones would cry, I know exactly which ones. It breaks my heart more than the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Mark change any plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd been talking about getting engaged at Christmas. I'd still want that, honestly more, because family is what you'd hang on to. But the wedding would be in the village hall with a buffet.

I'd say **communities** must look after each other, not wait for government.

With **less than a month** saved, they'd struggle within weeks.

fieldNote: Nora expects to **lose her job** as village schools close.

steps.text: Move onto the family sheep farm to stop paying rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to prepare if people are sensible. I'd want villages to plan together. I'd keep my head and get on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'd see the closure coming. I'd be thirty-two, and I'd have time to get a qualification that keeps me with children, like special needs support. Mark's farm has until about 2034 before robots really change it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tools more for planning, so I'm not left behind. I'd take an evening course in special educational needs support over two years. And Mark and I would save harder, maybe a hundred a month, and get engaged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can plan. Like spring lambing, hard work but you know it's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said family a lot. Is that what you'd fall back on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, always. Mark's parents have the farm, my parents have a spare room. That's how it should be. I'd only go to the government if everything else had gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Sunday school and the church?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching Sunday school, that's not about money. If anything, people would come more if things got hard. The church kept this village going through foot and mouth, my mum says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to do it properly, and children should come first. I'd say small schools deserve a fair chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels manageable for me, but not for the school. I think Ashby Green closes either way, AI or no AI, the numbers are falling. I'd be thirty-seven, maybe married with a child, and needing a job near the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching, try for the head's job when Mrs Pryce retires, and use AI for the paperwork side. I'd get married and start a family in two or three years. I'd look at running a small forest school on the farm, outdoor lessons for little ones, as a side business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a hopeful way. Like planting the vegetable patch with the children, you don't know what comes up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A forest school on a farm, would that survive the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so. Parents would pay for their children to be outdoors with a real person, getting muddy. It's the opposite of a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why is the school closing either way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Houses in the village sell to retired couples from the city. No young families, no children. AI won't change that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because the school would close and we'd have no money and no time. What would help is keeping small schools open, and real apprenticeships or courses near home, so you don't have to move to a city to retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about housing. Our village is losing children because young families can't buy here, and that's killing the school faster than any computer.
